extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent applicants and practitioners (prosecuting attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating written description, means-plus-function, claim scope changes, and new-matter issues under 35 U.S.C. 112 (and related statutes) during patent examination and prosecution. Covers examiner burdens, required findings for rejections, treatment of priority/interference support, and permissible amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on priority under 35 U.S.C. 119
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 119(a) or (e), the claims in a U.S. application are entitled to the benefit of a foreign priority date or the filing date of a provisional application if the corresponding foreign application or provisional application supports the claims in the manner required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must determine whether the earlier application provides written description support for the subject matter of the claims; see cited cases (In re Ziegler; Kawai v. Metlesics; In re Gosteli). If earlier application lacks requisite 112(a) support, priority benefit is not proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for a claim corresponding to a count in an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: In an interference proceeding, the claim corresponding to a count must be supported by the specification in the manner provided by 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a party seeks benefit of an earlier-filed U.S. application in an interference, the earlier application must meet the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) for the subject matter of the count. A broad generic disclosure to a class is not necessarily sufficient to describe a specific compound within the class (Fields v. Conover; Hyatt v. Boone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Original claim not sufficiently described (written description defects)
rubrics_metrics.description: An original claim may lack written description support when (1) the claim defines the invention in functional language specifying a desired result but the disclosure fails to sufficiently identify how the function is performed or the result is achieved; or (2) a broad genus claim is presented but the disclosure only describes a narrow species with no evidence that the genus is contemplated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere appearance of claim language in the specification ('ipsis verbis') does not necessarily satisfy the written description requirement. Examiner should consider whether one skilled in the art can recognize from the specification that the inventor was in possession of the claimed invention (Ariad; Enzo Biochem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness rejection for means‑ (or step‑) plus‑function limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim limitation expressed in means‑ or step‑plus‑function language 'shall be construed to cover the corresponding structure, material, or acts described in the specification and equivalents thereof' (35 U.S.C. 112(f) or pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, sixth paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification fails to disclose sufficient corresponding structure, materials, or acts that perform the entire claimed function, the limitation is indefinite because the applicant has failed to 'particularly point out and distinctly claim' the invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA para. 2) (In re Donaldson). Such a limitation also may lack adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) because an unbounded functional limitation would cover all ways of performing a function and indicate insufficient disclosure. See MPEP § 2181 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on the examiner regarding the written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry into whether the description requirement is met is a question of fact. A description as filed is presumed to be adequate unless and until sufficient evidence or reasoning to the contrary is presented by the examiner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner has the initial burden of presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in an applicant's disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims. Examiner must have a reasonable basis to challenge adequacy (In re Wertheim; In re Marzocchi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of rejection requirements for lack of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting a claim for lack of written description, the examiner must set forth express findings of fact which support the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings should (A) identify the claim limitation(s) at issue; and (B) establish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time of filing would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure as filed. A general allegation of 'unpredictability in the art' is insufficient. A simple, specific statement pointing out lack of apparent support may be sufficient where appropriate. See MPEP § 2163 and Hyatt v. Dudas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggesting amendments when rejecting for lack of written description
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, examiners should suggest amendments to the claims which can be supported by the application's written description, while being mindful of the prohibition against adding new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested amendments should stay within the original disclosure and not introduce new matter; see Rasmussen for guidance on permissible amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of applicant's reply before repeating a 112(a) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon reply by applicant, before repeating any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre‑AIA equivalent) for lack of written description, the examiner must review the basis for the rejection in view of the record as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the whole record (including amendments, arguments, and evidence submitted) demonstrates that the written description requirement is satisfied, do not repeat the rejection. If the record still does not demonstrate adequacy, repeat the rejection, fully respond to applicant's rebuttal arguments, and properly treat any further showings submitted in the reply. Affidavits relevant to written description must be thoroughly analyzed and discussed in the next Office action (In re Alton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes to scope of claims after filing (general written description principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to meet the written description requirement commonly arises when claims are changed after filing to broaden or narrow claim breadth, alter numerical ranges, or use language not synonymous with terminology in the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To comply with 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and to be entitled to an earlier priority or filing date under 35 U.S.C. 119, 120, or 365(c), each claim limitation must be expressly, implicitly, or inherently supported in the originally filed disclosure. See MPEP § 2163 for examination guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening claim — omission of a limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation can raise whether the inventor had possession of a broader, more generic invention; a claim that omits an element which applicant describes as essential or critical in the original disclosure does not comply with the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should consider language in the specification that describes an element as 'the only possible location' or 'outside the stated purpose of the invention' as indicating that omission broadens beyond inventor's possession (Gentry Gallery; Tronzo; In re Wilder). Such omission may also give rise to 112(b) indefiniteness or enablement issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadening claim — addition of a generic claim (genus supported by species)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed genus may be supported by a sufficient description of a representative number of species; a single species may support a genus only if the disclosure 'indicates that the patentee has invented species sufficient to constitute the gen[us]'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When there is substantial variation within the genus, a sufficient variety of species must be described to reflect that variation. Disclosure of only one species is inadequate when ordinary artisans could not predict operability of other species. However, in some situations one species may suffice (Enzo Biochem; In re Curtis; In re Rasmussen). Consider unpredictability in the art and whether specification teaches against other species (AbbVie; Tronzo; In re Gosteli).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowing or subgeneric claim changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducing claim changes that narrow claims by adding elements or limitations not supported in the as‑filed disclosure can violate the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'laundry list' disclosure of many moieties does not describe every species. Subgenus claims may be acceptable or not depending on whether the specification reasonably communicates the subgenus to those skilled in the art (Fujikawa; In re Ruschig; Rozbicki v. Chiang; Ex parte Sorenson; In re Smith). Each case is fact‑specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range limitations — changing numerical ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis of changing numerical range limitations must account for which ranges one skilled in the art would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims with open‑ended limits (e.g., 'at least 35%') that read on embodiments outside disclosed ranges may fail written description, whereas narrower ranges bounded within disclosed ranges may be acceptable (In re Wertheim; Purdue Pharma; Union Oil v. Atl. Richfield). Consider whether the specification shows the inventors considered particular ratios or ranges as part of their invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of written description requirement to new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of written description generally arises with respect to subject matter of a claim; adding or amending the abstract, specification, or drawings to include content not described in the application as filed raises a new matter issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 35 U.S.C. 132 prohibits introducing new matter into the disclosure; 35 U.S.C. 251 prohibits introducing new matter into an application for reissue. If new subject matter is added, examiner should object under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251 and require cancellation of the new matter. If new matter is added to claims, reject under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). Examiner should still consider added subject matter in prior art rejections since the new matter rejection may be overcome by applicant (In re Rasmussen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and review of new matter objections/rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification is amended to add new matter, make an objection; if claims contain new matter, make a rejection. Rejections are appealable to the Patent Trial and Appeal Board; objections/requirements to delete new matter are subject to supervisory review by petition (37 CFR 1.181).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both claims and specification contain new matter with both rejection and objection, the issue is appealable and should not be decided by petition. When amendments are filed in reply to an objection or rejection under 112(a), the entire application should be studied to determine whether new matter is involved; applicant should point out support for any amendments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed subject matter disclosed only in claims (antecedent/disclosure issues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if an original claim discloses material not disclosed in the remainder of the specification, the applicant may amend the specification to include the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.44 may be used where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification (In re Benno).

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description are not new matter (rephrasing permitted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere rephrasing of a passage does not constitute new matter; a rewording that preserves the same meaning is permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including dictionary or art‑recognized definitions known at filing may not be new matter. However, if multiple definitions exist for a term and a specific definition is later added, the original application must make clear the intended definition to avoid new matter or lack of written description (In re Anderson; Schering Corp. v. Amgen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious error corrections do not constitute new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to correct an obvious error does not constitute new matter where one skilled in the art would recognize both the error and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: where a foreign priority document is of record, applicant may not rely on that document to support correction of an error in the pending U.S. application unless the U.S. application explicitly incorporates the foreign document by reference. See Ex parte Bondiou and 37 CFR 1.55/1.57 guidance for inadvertently omitted portions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent function, theory, or advantage (doctrine of inherency)
rubrics_metrics.description: By disclosing a device that inherently performs a function or has a property, the patent application necessarily discloses that function, theory, or advantage even though it says nothing explicit concerning it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application may later be amended to recite the function/theory/advantage without introducing prohibited new matter (In re Reynolds; In re Smythe; Yeda Research v. Abbott). To establish inherency, extrinsic evidence must show the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; inherency may not be established by probabilities or possibilities.
